marking_schemes.question_text: Define moment of force.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: The turning effect of force (on a body pivoted) about an axis/fixed point/ a point or the product of magnitude of force and the perpendicular distance of line of action of force from the axis of rotation/fulcrum or moment = F × d where d = perpendicular distance between the point of application of force and axis of rotation / fulcrum.
key_points: Turning effect of force about an axis/pivot
Moment = Force × perpendicular distance from line of action to axis of rotation/fulcrum
marking_schemes.model_answer: Moment of force is the turning effect of a force about an axis or fixed point, equal to the product of the magnitude of the force and the perpendicular distance of the line of action of the force from the axis of rotation or fulcrum.
common_errors: Wrote 'point' of application instead of 'line' of action
Did not mention perpendicular distance, some wrote displacement
Wrote only 'turning effect' without mentioning axis of rotation or fulcrum
Wrote turning effect of a body instead of turning effect of force
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Explain the difference between distance and perpendicular distance and between point and line of application of force. Train students to write definitions in statement form instead of a formula.

marking_schemes.question_text: Write the relationship between the SI and CGS unit of moment of force.
marking_schemes.correct_answer: 1 N m = 10^7 dyn cm or 1 dyn cm = 10^-7 N m
marking_schemes.scheme_text: 1 N m = 10^7 dyn cm or 1 dyn cm = 10^-7 N m
key_points: 1 N m = 10^7 dyn cm
marking_schemes.model_answer: 1 N m = 10^7 dyn cm, or equivalently 1 dyn cm = 10^-7 N m.
common_errors: Wrote 1 N m = 10^7 erg instead of dyn-cm
Wrote 1 J = 10^7 dyn
Related SI and CGS units of force instead of moment of force
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Clarify the difference between force units and moment of force units.

marking_schemes.question_text: Define a kilowatt hour. How is it related to joule?
marking_schemes.scheme_text: One kilowatt hour is the energy spent/ or work done by a source of power 1kW in one hour (1000 W in 3600 s) Or it is the work done when 1 kW power is consumed for one hour or any statement to this effect. 1kW h = 3.6 x 10^6 J or 1 kW h = 3.6 M J
key_points: kWh is energy spent/work done by 1kW power source in one hour
marking_schemes.model_answer: One kilowatt hour is the energy consumed or work done by a source of power 1 kW operating for one hour (1000 W for 3600 s). 1 kW h = 3.6 × 10^6 J = 3.6 MJ.
common_errors: Did not mention it is energy consumed/required, wrote power instead
Comprehended 1kWh as 1 watt energy consumed in 1 hour
Multiplied by 10^3 instead of correct conversion
Errors converting 1kWh to J or MJ
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Explain the derivation between kWh and joule; give practice on conversions.

marking_schemes.question_text: A satellite revolves around a planet in a circular orbit. What is the work done by the satellite at any instant? Give a reason.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Zero. Force/centripetal force (of gravity) is always perpendicular to the displacement. OR W = Fd cos90; W = 0
key_points: Work done = zero
Centripetal/gravitational force is always perpendicular to displacement
marking_schemes.model_answer: The work done by the satellite at any instant is zero, because the centripetal force (gravitational force) acting on it is always perpendicular to its displacement (W = Fd cos90° = 0).
common_errors: Wrote displacement as zero instead of recognizing force is perpendicular to displacement at any instant
Overlooked the phrase 'work at any instant'
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Clarify that displacement is not zero in uniform circular motion, but it is perpendicular to the centripetal force at all times.

marking_schemes.question_text: Identify the class of the lever shown in the diagram below (fulcrum F, load L, effort E on a straight bar).
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Class III
key_points: Lever shown is Class III lever
marking_schemes.model_answer: The lever shown is a Class III lever.
common_errors: Some candidates did not identify the class of lever correctly
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Help students develop correct identification of lever classes through diagrams.

marking_schemes.question_text: How is it possible to increase the M.A. of the above lever without increasing its length?
marking_schemes.scheme_text: By shifting effort away from the fulcrum/ towards the load Or Shifting load towards effort/decreasing the load arm.
key_points: Shift effort away from fulcrum (towards load)
Or shift load towards effort, decreasing the load arm
marking_schemes.model_answer: By shifting the effort away from the fulcrum (towards the load), or by shifting the load towards the effort, thereby decreasing the load arm — without changing the overall length of the lever.
common_errors: Wrote memorized answer 'by increasing effort arm' without addressing the 'without increasing length' condition
Wrote 'by increasing load or decreasing effort' without realizing effort changes proportionately with load
Wrote 'change position of load and effort' without realizing the class of lever would change
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Clarify different ways of increasing/decreasing effort arm within a fixed lever length.

marking_schemes.question_text: Give one example of each when: Chemical energy changes into electrical energy.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Dry cell
key_points: Dry cell converts chemical energy to electrical energy
marking_schemes.model_answer: Dry cell (chemical energy converts to electrical energy).
common_errors: Confused between 'cell in use' and 'charging of a cell'
Gave vague answers
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Discuss maximum possible types of energy conversion in class.

marking_schemes.question_text: Give one example of each when: Electrical energy changes into sound energy.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Loudspeaker / Electric bell
key_points: Loudspeaker or electric bell converts electrical energy to sound energy
marking_schemes.model_answer: Loudspeaker or Electric bell (electrical energy converts to sound energy).
common_errors: Wrote microphone instead of loudspeaker
Gave technically incorrect answers such as 'bell' instead of 'electric bell'
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Teach difference between microphone and speaker with respect to energy conversions.

marking_schemes.question_text: A crane 'A' lifts a heavy load in 5 seconds, whereas another crane 'B' does the same work in 2 seconds. Compare the power of crane 'A' to that of crane 'B'.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: PA/PB = WA/tA ÷ WB/tB ∴ PA/PB = WA/tA × tB/WB but WA = WB ∴ PA/PB = tB/tA ∴ PA : PB = 2 : 5 (Or any other correct method)
key_points: Power is inversely proportional to time for same work
PA : PB = tB : tA = 2 : 5
marking_schemes.model_answer: Since work done by both cranes is the same, power is inversely proportional to time taken. PA/PB = tB/tA = 2/5, so PA : PB = 2 : 5.
common_errors: Expressed answer in fractional form instead of ratio form
Did not get inverse proportion between power and time for same work
Wrote answer using > and < instead of ratio form
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Instruct students to answer comparisons in ratio form when data is available, clarifying which quantity is compared with which.

marking_schemes.question_text: A ray of light falls normally on a rectangular glass slab. Draw a ray diagram showing the path of the ray till it emerges out of the slab.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Ray with correct name and arrow marks carries marks — incident ray strikes normally, passes straight through undeviated, and emerges as emergent ray, both labelled with arrows.
key_points: Ray passes straight through the slab undeviated (normal incidence)
Incident and emergent rays clearly labelled with arrows
marking_schemes.model_answer: A ray incident normally on a rectangular glass slab passes straight through without bending, emerging parallel to and in line with the incident ray, both rays clearly labelled with arrows.
common_errors: Took ray normal at one surface but showed it bent at the other surface
Marked angle with second surface as 90°
Did not mark arrows on the rays
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Give adequate practice of drawing ray diagrams on rectangular glass slabs, both oblique and normal incidence. Instruct students to mark arrows on rays.

marking_schemes.question_text: Complete the path of the monochromatic light ray AB incident on the surface PQ of the equilateral glass prism PQR till it emerges out of the prism due to refraction.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Diagram showing ray AB refracting at PQ (bending towards normal, i>r), travelling through the prism, and refracting again at PR (bending away from normal) as it emerges, with angle of incidence i, refraction angles r and r', and emergence angle e all marked.
key_points: Ray bends towards normal on entering at PQ
Ray bends away from normal on emerging at PR
Arrows marked on all rays
marking_schemes.model_answer: The ray AB refracts at surface PQ (bending towards the normal since entering a denser medium), travels through the prism, and refracts again at PR (bending away from the normal) as it emerges into air.
common_errors: Showed dispersion instead of simple refraction (question specifies monochromatic light)
Missed marking arrows on the rays
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Explain the difference between monochromatic and polychromatic light clearly. Teach students how to draw the normal to an inclined surface.

marking_schemes.question_text: Where should an object be placed in front of a convex lens in order to get an enlarged real image?
marking_schemes.correct_answer: Object is placed between F and 2F Or at F
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Object is placed between F and 2F Or at F
key_points: Object placed between F and 2F (or at F) for enlarged real image
marking_schemes.model_answer: The object should be placed between F and 2F (or at F) of the convex lens.
common_errors: Confused between F1 and 2F1, F2 and 2F2
Confused between virtual and real image positions
Drew ray diagram when not asked
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Familiarise students with related terminology, e.g. centre of curvature or 2F with respect to focal length.

marking_schemes.question_text: Where should an object be placed in front of a convex lens in order to get an enlarged virtual image?
marking_schemes.correct_answer: Object is placed between F and O / within the focal length/between lens and F
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Object is placed between F and O / within the focal length/between lens and F
key_points: Object placed between F and O (within focal length) for enlarged virtual image
marking_schemes.model_answer: The object should be placed between the lens (O) and the focal point F, i.e., within the focal length of the convex lens.
common_errors: Confusion between F and 2F positions
Drew ray diagram instead of stating position
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Tell students that if a descriptive question is asked, the answer cannot be in the form of a diagram alone.

marking_schemes.question_text: A pond appears to be 2.7 m deep. If the refractive index of water is 4/3, find the actual depth of the pond.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Apparent depth = 2.7 m; µ = actual depth [Real depth]/Apparent depth; 4/3 = X/2.7; X = 4/3 × 2.7 = 3.6 m. (Any other correct method)
key_points: μ = Real depth/Apparent depth
marking_schemes.model_answer: μ = Real depth / Apparent depth, so 4/3 = X/2.7, giving X = 4/3 × 2.7 = 3.6 m. The actual depth of the pond is 3.6 m.
common_errors: Wrote incorrect formula
Took shift as apparent depth
Calculation errors
Did not write the unit in the final answer
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Point out the difference between real depth, apparent depth and shift clearly. Advise students to write data before substituting values, and to write final answer with unit.

marking_schemes.question_text: The wavelengths for the light of red and blue colours are nearly 7.8 x 10^-7 m and 4.8 x 10^-7 m respectively. Which colour has the greater speed in a vacuum?
marking_schemes.correct_answer: In vacuum, both have the same speed.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: In vacuum, both have the same speed.
key_points: Both colours travel at the same speed in vacuum
marking_schemes.model_answer: In vacuum, both red and blue light travel at the same speed, since the speed of light in vacuum is independent of wavelength/colour.
common_errors: Wrote blue or red randomly without knowing the concept
Treated wavelengths as speed
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Tell students that the velocity of light of all colours in vacuum or air remains the same and changes only when the medium changes.

marking_schemes.question_text: The wavelengths for the light of red and blue colours are nearly 7.8 x 10^-7 m and 4.8 x 10^-7 m respectively. Which colour has a greater speed in glass?
marking_schemes.correct_answer: In glass, red light has greater speed.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: In glass, red light has greater speed. (Or any correct statement)
key_points: Red light has greater speed in glass (longer wavelength, less bending/refraction)
marking_schemes.model_answer: In glass, red light has a greater speed than blue light, since red has a longer wavelength and bends less on refraction.
common_errors: Did not establish relation between speed and wavelength in a medium
Wrote 'blue' randomly
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Explain how speed relates to wavelength when light passes into a denser medium.

marking_schemes.question_text: Draw a graph between displacement from mean position and time for a body executing free vibration in a vacuum.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Graph shows a sine-wave type curve, symmetric about the time axis, with amplitude +a and -a marked, axes labelled Displacement (m) and Time (s), constant amplitude throughout (no damping).
key_points: Axes labelled Displacement (m) vs Time (s)
Sinusoidal curve equally spaced above and below mean position (X-axis)
Constant, undiminishing amplitude (free vibration, no damping)
marking_schemes.model_answer: A sine-curve graph with time on the X-axis and displacement on the Y-axis, oscillating symmetrically between +a and -a with constant amplitude throughout, representing free (undamped) vibration.
common_errors: Axes not labelled
X-axis not taken as mean position
Drew single curve instead of full wave
Drew graph of minimum deviation vs angle of incidence mislabelled as displacement-time
Drew only positive quadrant without negative amplitude
Drew damped vibration graph instead of free vibration
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Clarify that in free vibrations, amplitude remains the same above and below the X-axis. Explain difference between free and damped vibration graphs.

marking_schemes.question_text: A sound wave travelling in water has wavelength 0.4 m. Is this wave audible in air? (The speed of sound in water = 1400 ms-1)
marking_schemes.scheme_text: V = fλ; 1400 = f × 0.4; f = 3500 Hz; Yes, it is audible (frequency remains constant across media and lies within the audible range 20 Hz–20,000 Hz).
key_points: V = fλ
Frequency is constant across media; 3500 Hz lies within audible range, so it is audible
marking_schemes.model_answer: Using V = fλ: 1400 = f × 0.4, so f = 3500 Hz. Since frequency remains constant when a wave passes between media, and 3500 Hz lies within the audible range (20 Hz–20,000 Hz), the wave is audible in air.
common_errors: Simply wrote 'audible in air' or 'not audible' without calculating frequency
Wrote incorrect unit of frequency
Used echo velocity formula incorrectly
Were not aware of the audible frequency range
Treated calculated 'time' as time period incorrectly
Used speed of sound in water as 336 m/s incorrectly (that is speed in air)
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Acquaint students with the relation velocity = frequency × wavelength, and the audible range of frequency.

marking_schemes.question_text: Why does stone lying in the sun get heated up much more than water lying for the same duration of time?
marking_schemes.scheme_text: The specific heat capacity of water is very much higher than that of stone. So, temperature of stone increases quickly by absorbing comparatively less heat than water.
key_points: Specific heat capacity of water is much higher than that of stone
Stone's temperature rises quickly by absorbing less heat compared to water
marking_schemes.model_answer: The specific heat capacity of water is much higher than that of stone. So for the same amount of heat absorbed, the temperature of the stone rises much more than that of water in the same time.
common_errors: Related answer to difference in absorption of heat or heat capacity instead of specific heat capacity
Wrote stone takes less time because it is a good conductor instead of referencing specific heat capacity
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Point out the difference between specific heat capacity and heat capacity.

marking_schemes.question_text: Why is it not advisable to use a piece of copper wire as fuse wire in an electric circuit?
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Copper has low resistivity and high melting point whereas fuse wire should have low melting point and high resistivity.
key_points: Copper has low resistivity and high melting point
Fuse wire should have low melting point and high resistivity
marking_schemes.model_answer: Copper has low resistivity and a high melting point, whereas a good fuse wire needs low melting point and high resistivity so that it melts and breaks the circuit quickly during excess current. Hence copper is unsuitable as a fuse wire.
common_errors: Wrote about resistance instead of resistivity
Gave low melting point of copper as reason for not using it (incorrect, copper has high melting point)
Wrote characteristics of fuse only without comparing with copper
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Discuss fuse, its characteristics and uses in detail; explain how fuse wire compares with copper wire.

marking_schemes.question_text: Calculate the total resistance across AB: (3Ω and 6Ω in parallel combination, in series with 5Ω)
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Parallel combination: R1 = (6×3)/(6+3) ∴ R1 = 2Ω; R = 2 + 5 = 7 Ω
key_points: Parallel resistance R1 = (6×3)/(6+3) = 2Ω
Total R = R1 + 5 = 7 Ω
marking_schemes.model_answer: For the parallel combination of 3Ω and 6Ω: R1 = (6×3)/(6+3) = 2Ω. Total resistance = 2 + 5 = 7 Ω.
common_errors: Incorrect substitution in parallel combination formula
Calculation errors
Units not written in final answer
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Give adequate practice of numerical problems based on combination of resistors.

marking_schemes.question_text: Two metallic blocks P and Q having masses in ratio 2:1 are supplied with the same amount of heat. If their temperatures rise by same degree, compare their specific heat capacities.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: mP = 2m (say), mq = m, ∆tp = ∆tq = ∆t (say). Heat given to P = Heat given to Q: mp×cp×∆t = m×cq×∆t; 2m×cp×∆t = m×cq×∆t (correct formula with substitution); Cp/Cq = 1/2; Cp:Cq = 1:2
key_points: Set masses as 2m and m
Equal heat and equal temperature rise gives 2m×cp = m×cq
Cp:Cq = 1:2
marking_schemes.model_answer: Let mP = 2m, mQ = m, with equal heat Q and equal temperature rise ∆t for both. Since Q = mc∆t, 2m×cP×∆t = m×cQ×∆t, giving cP/cQ = 1/2, i.e., cP : cQ = 1 : 2.
common_errors: Incorrect substitution for masses
Compared heat capacities instead of specific heat capacities
Substituted masses correctly but failed to express specific heat capacities in ratio form
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Train students to draw conclusions about proportions of remaining quantities when some quantities are kept constant, and to express comparisons in ratio form.

marking_schemes.question_text: When a current carrying conductor is placed in a magnetic field, it experiences a mechanical force. What should be the angle between the magnetic field and the length of the conductor so that the force experienced is zero?
marking_schemes.scheme_text: 0° / zero or parallel (180,360…...)
key_points: Angle = 0° (or 180°/360°, i.e. conductor parallel to field) for zero force
marking_schemes.model_answer: 0° (the conductor is parallel to the magnetic field), or equivalently 180°/360°.
common_errors: Answered with a coil in mind instead of a straight conductor
Could not state the angles correctly
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Demonstrate the force experienced by a current carrying straight conductor and a coil for better understanding.

marking_schemes.question_text: When a current carrying conductor is placed in a magnetic field, it experiences a mechanical force. What should be the angle between the magnetic field and the length of the conductor so that the force experienced is maximum?
marking_schemes.scheme_text: 90° or Perpendicular (270….)
key_points: Angle = 90° (conductor perpendicular to field) for maximum force
marking_schemes.model_answer: 90° (the conductor is perpendicular to the magnetic field), or equivalently 270°.
common_errors: Confused with coil scenario instead of straight conductor
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Same as above — reinforce distinction between straight conductor and coil in a magnetic field.

marking_schemes.question_text: A nucleus 84X202 of an element emits an alpha particle followed by a beta particle. The final nucleus is aYb. Find a and b.
key_points: Alpha emission: 84X202 → 82Z198 + 2He4
Beta emission: 82Z198 → 83Y198 + -1β0
Final: a=83, b=198
marking_schemes.model_answer: Alpha emission: 84X202 → 82Z198 + 2He4. Beta emission: 82Z198 → 83Y198 + -1β0. Therefore a = 83 and b = 198.
common_errors: Did not explicitly state which value is 'a' and which is 'b', leaving it as 83Y198 for examiner to interpret
Interchanged atomic and mass numbers
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Lay stress on practicing balanced nuclear equations and correctly identifying atomic number and mass number.

marking_schemes.question_text: The diagram below shows a loop of wire carrying current I. What is the magnetic polarity of the loop that faces us?
marking_schemes.scheme_text: South
key_points: Polarity facing us is South
marking_schemes.model_answer: South pole faces us.
common_errors: Wrote North instead of South
Wrote polarity as 'south to north' or 'north to south' which is incorrect phrasing
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Use right-hand rule to determine polarity of current loop.

marking_schemes.question_text: With respect to the diagram how can we increase the strength of the magnetic field produced by this loop?
marking_schemes.correct_answer: By increasing the strength of the current.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: By increasing the strength of the current.
key_points: Increase the current strength (number of turns is fixed in this diagram)
marking_schemes.model_answer: By increasing the strength (magnitude) of the current flowing through the loop, since the number of turns shown in the diagram remains fixed.
common_errors: Did not account for the fact that the number of turns is fixed, and incorrectly wrote 'increase number of turns'
Wrote vague answer like 'increasing the magnetic strength'
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Point out that the diagram shows a single loop with a fixed number of turns; the only variable is current strength.

marking_schemes.question_text: The figure below shows a simple pendulum of mass 200 g. It is displaced from the mean position A to the extreme position B. The potential energy at the position A is zero. At the position B the pendulum bob is raised by 5 m. What is the potential energy of the pendulum at the position B?
marking_schemes.scheme_text: PE = mgh = 0.2 x 10 x 5 = 10 J
key_points: Convert mass to kg (0.2 kg)
marking_schemes.model_answer: PE = mgh = 0.2 kg × 10 m/s² × 5 m = 10 J.
common_errors: Did not convert mass from grams to kg, leading to incorrect answer
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Lay stress on conversion of units.

marking_schemes.question_text: The figure below shows a simple pendulum of mass 200 g, displaced from mean position A to extreme position B (raised by 5 m), with point C between A and B. What is the total mechanical energy at point C?
key_points: By conservation of energy, total mechanical energy at C equals total mechanical energy at B = 10 J
marking_schemes.model_answer: By the principle of conservation of mechanical energy, the total mechanical energy at C is the same as at B, which is 10 J.
common_errors: Did not realize the principle of conservation of energy applies
Simply wrote 'total mechanical energy = P.E. + K.E.' without giving the exact value
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Give adequate practice on diagram-based/conceptual questions to apply conservation of energy.

marking_schemes.question_text: What is the speed of the bob at the position A when released from B? (Take g = 10 ms-2 and there is no loss of energy.)
key_points: Use conservation of energy: ½mv² = mgh or v² = 2E/m
marking_schemes.model_answer: Using conservation of energy, ½mv² = mgh, so v = √(2gh) = √(2×10×5) = 10 m/s.
common_errors: Wrote unit of acceleration instead of velocity
Could not apply conservation of mechanical energy correctly
Some wrote v² = 10 m/s incorrectly
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Train students to mention the principle involved while solving numericals.

marking_schemes.question_text: With reference to the direction of action, how does a centripetal force differ from a centrifugal force during uniform circular motion?
marking_schemes.correct_answer: Centripetal force acts radially inward and centrifugal force acts radially outward.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Centripetal force acts radially inward and centrifugal force acts radially outward.
key_points: Centripetal force acts radially inward
Centrifugal force acts radially outward
marking_schemes.model_answer: Centripetal force acts radially inward (towards the centre of the circular path), whereas centrifugal force acts radially outward (away from the centre).
common_errors: Wrote only 'inside' or 'outside' instead of 'radially inside' or 'radially outside'
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Clarify the concept of centripetal and centrifugal forces.

marking_schemes.question_text: Is centrifugal force the force of reaction of centripetal force?
marking_schemes.scheme_text: No.
key_points: Centrifugal force is NOT the reaction force of centripetal force
marking_schemes.model_answer: No, centrifugal force is not the reaction force of centripetal force.
common_errors: Most candidates answered correctly; a few gave vague answers
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Reinforce the distinction between a reaction force pair and centripetal/centrifugal forces.

marking_schemes.question_text: Compare the magnitudes of centripetal and centrifugal force.
key_points: Centripetal and centrifugal forces are equal in magnitude (1:1) but opposite in direction
marking_schemes.model_answer: Centripetal and centrifugal forces are equal in magnitude, i.e., in the ratio 1:1, though opposite in direction.
common_errors: Explained centripetal and centrifugal forces but did not compare their magnitudes
Wrote that centripetal force is greater/more than centrifugal force
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Teach students that centripetal and centrifugal forces are equal in magnitude but opposite in direction.

marking_schemes.question_text: A block and tackle system of pulleys has velocity ratio 4. Draw a neat, labelled diagram of the system indicating clearly the points of application and direction of load and effort.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Diagram: A block and tackle system with a fixed pulley block (2 pulleys) at top and a movable pulley block (2 pulleys) below, string running from fixed support through the pulleys with effort applied upward at the free end, and load hanging from the movable block, giving velocity ratio 4.
key_points: Fixed support shown
Strands drawn taut and correctly connected
Direction of load and effort clearly marked
Correct number of pulleys/strands for V.R. = 4
marking_schemes.model_answer: A block and tackle system with two pulleys in the fixed block and two in the movable block, connected by a continuous string anchored to a fixed support, with effort applied upward at the free end of the string and the load suspended from the movable block, giving a velocity ratio of 4.
common_errors: No fixed support shown
Strands drawn loose
Incorrect connections shown
Directions of load and/or effort not marked
Rough sketches of pulleys drawn
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Train students to draw pulley-related diagrams and mark tension force in strings, with practice on odd and even velocity ratios.

marking_schemes.question_text: What will be its V.R. if the weight of the movable block is doubled?
marking_schemes.correct_answer: Velocity Ratio does not change and remains 4.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Velocity Ratio does not change and remains 4.
key_points: V.R. depends on the number of strands/pulleys, not on weight of movable block
V.R. remains 4
marking_schemes.model_answer: Velocity ratio depends only on the number of pulleys/strands supporting the movable block, not on the weight of the movable block. So the V.R. remains unchanged at 4.
common_errors: Wrote that V.R. becomes half or double, which is incorrect
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Clarify the concept of velocity ratio for a given machine design and the effect (or lack thereof) of weight of parts of the machine on velocity ratio.

marking_schemes.question_text: A diver in water looks obliquely at an object AB in air. Does the object appear taller, shorter or of the same size to the diver?
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Taller
key_points: Object appears taller to the diver
marking_schemes.model_answer: The object appears taller to the diver.
common_errors: Could not establish the relation between image size and change in medium
Considered light passing from denser to rarer medium incorrectly
Wrote 'shorter' or 'of the same size' incorrectly
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Train students to draw diagrams applying laws of refraction at every surface when the ray changes medium.

marking_schemes.question_text: Show the path of two rays AC & AD starting from the tip of the object as it travels towards the diver in water and hence obtain the image of the object.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Diagram showing rays AC and AD from tip A refracting at the water surface (bending away from normal on entering denser medium water from air... actually entering water from air side towards diver), extended backward as dotted lines to meet at a point above A, forming a virtual, taller image, with the diver's eye shown receiving the diverging refracted rays.
key_points: Rays bend at the air-water interface following laws of refraction
Refracted rays extended backward with dotted lines to locate virtual image
Image formed is virtual, taller, and located above the actual object position
marking_schemes.model_answer: Rays AC and AD from point A refract at the interface as they enter water, bending according to the laws of refraction. Extending the refracted rays backward (dotted lines) shows they appear to diverge from a point higher than A, forming a virtual, taller image visible to the diver's eye.
common_errors: Did not mark arrows on rays
Showed partial reflection along with refraction
Did not show extension of rays and dotted image
Showed incorrect image position and incorrect refraction
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Point out that virtual images should be dotted and apparent intersections shown by dotted lines. Lay stress on drawing arrows on rays before and after refraction.

marking_schemes.question_text: Complete the path of the ray AB through the glass prism PQR till it emerges out of the prism. Given the critical angle of the glass as 42°. (Prism has angle P = 30°, right angle at Q, ray AB enters normally at QR from below)
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Ray travelling undeviated at QR; Total Internal Reflection at surface PR (angle of incidence 60° > critical angle 42°); Bending away (refraction) at PQ as it emerges.
key_points: Ray travels undeviated through QR (normal incidence)
Total internal reflection occurs at surface PR since angle of incidence (60°) exceeds critical angle (42°)
Ray refracts and bends away from normal as it emerges through PQ
marking_schemes.model_answer: The ray AB enters the prism undeviated at QR (normal incidence). At surface PR, since the angle of incidence (60°) exceeds the critical angle (42°), total internal reflection occurs. The reflected ray then strikes surface PQ and refracts, bending away from the normal as it emerges from the prism.
common_errors: Showed the ray entering the prism as bending (should be undeviated at normal incidence)
Did not mark angle of incidence
Showed the ray coming out un-deviated after total internal reflection
Showed refraction at the second surface incorrectly
Treated the prism as a right-angled isosceles prism
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Clarify sign convention, and the correct application of total internal reflection versus refraction based on critical angle.

marking_schemes.question_text: A lens of focal length 20 cm forms an inverted image at a distance 60 cm from the lens. Identify the lens.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Convex lens
key_points: Lens is a convex lens (since it forms a real, inverted image)
marking_schemes.model_answer: It is a convex lens, since it forms a real, inverted image.
common_errors: Barring a few, all candidates identified the lens correctly
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Teach students the method to identify a given lens from the description in the question.

marking_schemes.question_text: How far is the lens present in front of the object?
key_points: Apply lens formula 1/f = 1/v - 1/u with sign convention
u = -30 cm
marking_schemes.model_answer: Using 1/f = 1/v - 1/u with f = 20 cm, v = 60 cm: 1/u = 1/v - 1/f = 1/60 - 1/20 = -2/60, so u = -30 cm. The lens is 30 cm in front of the object.
common_errors: Incorrect sign convention
Incorrect substitution in the lens formula
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Clarify sign convention thoroughly and give adequate practice of numerical problems on the lens formula.

marking_schemes.question_text: Calculate the magnification of the image.
marking_schemes.model_answer: Magnification m = v/u = 60/(-30) = -2.
common_errors: Did not consider the sign convention
Some candidates wrote a unit for magnification (magnification is a pure ratio, unitless)
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Clarify that pure ratios such as magnification have no unit; explain concept of linear magnification for both types of lenses.

marking_schemes.question_text: Give reasons for the following: During the day, clouds appear white.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Due to greater size of particles of clouds all colours scatter equally/uniformly.
key_points: Cloud particles are larger in size
All colours of light scatter equally/uniformly, giving white appearance
marking_schemes.model_answer: Due to the greater size of the particles in clouds, all colours of light are scattered equally/uniformly, so clouds appear white.
common_errors: Used the term reflection or dispersion instead of scattering
Did not mention size of particles or uniform scattering
Confused white colour of clouds with white colour of sky at noon
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Lay stress on key words like dispersion and scattering; explain dependence of extent of scattering on wavelength of light.

marking_schemes.question_text: Give reasons for the following: During the day, sky appears blue.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Due to smaller size of particles of atmosphere blue with shorter wavelength scatters more than colours of longer wavelength.
key_points: Atmospheric particles are smaller in size
Blue light (shorter wavelength) scatters more than colours of longer wavelength
marking_schemes.model_answer: Due to the smaller size of atmospheric particles, blue light, having a shorter wavelength, scatters more than light of longer wavelengths, giving the sky its blue appearance.
common_errors: Did not compare the wavelengths in the explanation
Gave incorrect reasons
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Explain dependence of extent of scattering with respect to wavelength of light; give sufficient practice on conceptual/reasoning-based questions.

marking_schemes.question_text: Name the system which enables us to locate underwater objects by transmitting ultrasonic waves and detecting the reflecting impulse.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: SONAR/ Sound Navigation and Ranging
key_points: SONAR (Sound Navigation and Ranging)
marking_schemes.model_answer: SONAR (Sound Navigation and Ranging).
common_errors: Wrote the process as 'echo depth sounding' instead of naming the system SONAR
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Clarify the difference between a process and a system.

marking_schemes.question_text: What are acoustically measurable quantities related to pitch and loudness?
marking_schemes.correct_answer: For pitch – it is frequency. For loudness – it is intensity of sound.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: For pitch – it is frequency; For loudness – it is intensity of sound
key_points: Pitch is measured by frequency
Loudness is measured by intensity of sound
marking_schemes.model_answer: Pitch is related to the measurable quantity frequency, while loudness is related to the measurable quantity intensity of sound.
common_errors: Wrote the unit for pitch instead of the quantity
Gave 'quality' as the answer for pitch
Wrote 'amplitude' for loudness instead of intensity
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Explain the subjective nature of characteristics of sound versus the objective physical quantities on which they depend, with examples.

marking_schemes.question_text: When a tuning fork [vibrating] is held close to ear, one hears a faint hum. The same [vibrating tuning fork] is held such that its stem is in contact with the table surface, then one hears a loud sound. Explain.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: A tuning fork held close to ear, disturbs a small volume of air and hence, sound heard is faint. When the handle of the vibrating tuning fork is held against table it sets up forced vibrations in the tabletop. As tabletop has a large surface area large volume of air is set into vibration transmitting more energy thereby producing loud sound.
key_points: Tuning fork alone disturbs only a small volume of air, giving faint sound
Contact with table sets up forced vibrations in the tabletop
Large surface area of table sets a large volume of air vibrating, transmitting more energy, producing loud sound
marking_schemes.model_answer: A tuning fork held close to the ear disturbs only a small volume of air, so the sound heard is faint. When its stem touches the table, it sets up forced vibrations in the tabletop. Since the tabletop has a large surface area, a large volume of air is set into vibration, transmitting more energy and producing a loud sound.
common_errors: Related the explanation to resonance rather than surface area of the table
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Explain about free vibrations, forced vibrations, and resonance; discuss conceptual problems around this distinction.

marking_schemes.question_text: A man standing in front of a vertical cliff fires a gun. He hears the echo after 3.5 seconds. On moving closer to the cliff by 84 m, he hears the echo after 3 seconds. Calculate the distance of the cliff from the initial position of the man.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Let distance between cliff and initial position of man = x m. Total distance travelled by sound = 2x, time = 3.5 s, Speed = 2x/3.5 ...(1). After moving 84 m closer: distance = 2(x-84), time = 3 s, Speed = 2(x-84)/3 ...(2). From 1 and 2: 2x/3.5 = 2(x-84)/3; 7x - 588 = 6x; x = 588 m. The required distance = 588 m.
key_points: Set up equations for speed of sound before and after moving closer
Equate the two speed expressions
Solve to get x = 588 m
marking_schemes.model_answer: Let x be the initial distance to the cliff. Speed of sound = 2x/3.5 = 2(x−84)/3. Cross-multiplying: 3(2x) = 3.5×2(x−84), i.e., 6x = 7x − 588, so x = 588 m. The distance of the cliff from the man's initial position is 588 m.
common_errors: Formed correct equations but could not solve them correctly
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Give adequate practice on echo-based conceptual/numerical problems; advise students to draw a rough diagram for better comprehension and to frame correct equations.

marking_schemes.question_text: The diagram below shows the core of a transformer and its input (220 V A.C. Mains) and output (44 V A.C.) connections. State the material used for the core.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: laminated soft iron
key_points: Core material is laminated soft iron
marking_schemes.model_answer: Laminated soft iron.
common_errors: A few candidates stated the wrong material for the core
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: The construction and working of a transformer should be explained clearly to students.

marking_schemes.question_text: Copy and complete the diagram of the transformer by drawing input and output coils.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Diagram showing input coil (more turns, connected to 220V A.C. mains) and output coil (fewer turns, connected to 44V A.C. output) wound on the laminated soft iron core, correctly connected to the respective terminals.
key_points: Input coil with more turns wound on core, connected to 220V terminals
Output coil with fewer turns wound on core, connected to 44V output terminals
Coils correctly connected to shown terminals
marking_schemes.model_answer: The primary (input) coil with more turns is wound on one arm of the core and connected to the 220 V A.C. mains terminals; the secondary (output) coil with fewer turns is wound on the other arm (or same core) and connected to the 44 V A.C. output terminals.
common_errors: Did not connect the coil to the terminals shown in the diagram
Showed coils in incorrect arms
Showed incorrect number of turns (more turns for less voltage and vice versa)
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Give sufficient practice of drawing labelled diagrams with clear explanation of the transformer's working.

marking_schemes.question_text: What are superconductors?
marking_schemes.scheme_text: A superconductor is a substance whose resistance is zero at temperature closer to absolute zero.
key_points: Substance with zero resistance
At temperatures close to absolute zero
marking_schemes.model_answer: A superconductor is a substance whose resistance becomes zero at temperatures close to absolute zero.
common_errors: Confused superconductors with semiconductors
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: In the definition of superconductors, use 'at temperatures closer to absolute zero' rather than the vague term 'very low resistance'.

marking_schemes.question_text: Calculate the current drawn by an appliance rated 110 W, 220 V when connected across 220 V supply.
key_points: P = VI
marking_schemes.model_answer: Using P = VI: I = P/V = 110/220 = 0.5 A.
common_errors: Errors in copying the given data
Calculation errors
Unit not written
Incorrect unit given
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Help students by giving regular practice of solving numericals; discuss variation of resistance with temperature separately.

marking_schemes.question_text: Name a substance whose resistance decreases with the increase in temperature.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Carbon/ silicon/germanium or a semi-conductor
key_points: Carbon, silicon, germanium, or any semiconductor
marking_schemes.model_answer: Carbon, silicon, or germanium (a semiconductor) — its resistance decreases with increase in temperature.
common_errors: Wrote random incorrect names such as galvanized rubber, metals, copper, aluminium, tungsten, constantan, manganin, nichrome
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Discuss variation of resistance with temperature in detail, distinguishing conductors from semiconductors.

marking_schemes.question_text: The diagram shows three resistors (3Ω, 1.5Ω in parallel combination, and 4Ω in series) connected across a cell of e.m.f. 1.8 V and internal resistance r, with a current of 0.3 A. Calculate the current through the 3Ω resistor.
key_points: Use current divider rule for parallel combination of 3Ω and 1.5Ω
marking_schemes.model_answer: Using the current divider rule for the 3Ω and 1.5Ω parallel combination: I3Ω = (0.3 × 1.5)/(3+1.5) = 0.45/4.5 = 0.1 A.
common_errors: Took potential difference across 3Ω as 1.8 V incorrectly
Incorrect calculation of external resistance
Incorrect formula used or calculation errors
Unit not written
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Explain combination of resistors in series and parallel thoroughly; give adequate practice of numerical/conceptual problems on resistor combinations.

marking_schemes.question_text: The diagram shows three resistors connected across a cell of e.m.f. 1.8 V and internal resistance r, with a current of 0.3 A. Calculate the internal resistance r.
key_points: R1 (parallel combination) = 1Ω
Total external resistance R = 1+4 = 5Ω
Apply E = I(R+r) to solve for r = 1Ω
marking_schemes.model_answer: Parallel combination R1 = (1.5×3)/(1.5+3) = 1Ω. Total external resistance R = 1 + 4 = 5Ω. Using E = I(R+r): 1.8 = 0.3(5+r), so r = 1.8/0.3 − 5 = 6 − 5 = 1Ω.
common_errors: Considered emf as the terminal voltage incorrectly
Wrote incorrect unit for the asked physical quantity
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Comparison of EMF, terminal voltage, and voltage drop should be explained in detail.

marking_schemes.question_text: Define heat capacity of a substance.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: The amount of heat energy absorbed to raise the temperature of a body by unit degree is called as heat capacity.
key_points: Heat capacity = heat energy needed to raise temperature of a body by 1 degree
marking_schemes.model_answer: Heat capacity is the amount of heat energy absorbed by a body to raise its temperature by one degree.
common_errors: Wrote the definition of specific heat capacity instead, assuming the substance to be water
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Clarify the difference between heat capacity and specific heat capacity.

marking_schemes.question_text: Write the SI unit of heat capacity.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: unit - J K^-1
key_points: SI unit is J K^-1 (joule per kelvin)
marking_schemes.model_answer: The SI unit of heat capacity is J K⁻¹ (joule per kelvin).
common_errors: Wrote the unit of specific heat capacity instead
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Insist on writing the SI unit of temperature as kelvin (K), e.g., J/K rather than J/°C.

marking_schemes.question_text: What is the relationship between heat capacity and specific heat capacity of a substance?
marking_schemes.correct_answer: Heat capacity = mass × specific heat capacity
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Heat capacity = mass × specific heat capacity
key_points: Heat capacity = mass × specific heat capacity
marking_schemes.model_answer: Heat capacity = mass × specific heat capacity of the substance.
common_errors: Wrote the relationship in symbols without giving the meaning of the symbols
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Encourage students to write relations between physical quantities in words, or give meanings of symbols if expressed symbolically.

marking_schemes.question_text: The diagram below shows the change of phases of a substance on a temperature vs time graph on heating the substance at a constant rate (A-B-C-D-E-F with plateaus at t1 and t2). Why is the slope of CD less than slope of AB?
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Specific heat capacity in liquid state is greater than specific heat capacity in solid state
key_points: Specific heat capacity of the substance in liquid state is greater than in solid state, so temperature rises more slowly for the same heat input
marking_schemes.model_answer: The slope of CD is less than that of AB because the specific heat capacity of the substance in its liquid state (CD) is greater than in its solid state (AB), so for the same rate of heat supply, the temperature rises more slowly during CD.
common_errors: Many candidates could not answer this correctly; related it incorrectly with time
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Point out how specific heat capacity is different for different states of matter; train students to read information from the graph and interpret it correctly.

marking_schemes.question_text: What is the boiling and melting point of the substance (from the given temperature vs time graph)?
marking_schemes.correct_answer: Boiling point t2 °C, Melting point t1 °C
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Boiling point t2 °C; Melting point t1 °C
key_points: Melting point = t1 °C (lower plateau, BC)
Boiling point = t2 °C (upper plateau, DE)
marking_schemes.model_answer: The melting point of the substance is t1 °C (corresponding to plateau BC), and the boiling point is t2 °C (corresponding to plateau DE).
common_errors: Wrote vague values such as 100°C, 90°C instead of t1/t2
Wrote 'BC', 'DE' as answers instead of temperature values
Interchanged melting point and boiling point values
Answered assuming the substance to be water
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Give more practice on graph-based questions in calorimetry.

marking_schemes.question_text: A piece of ice of mass 60 g is dropped into 140 g of water at 50°C. Calculate the final temperature of water when all the ice has melted. (Assume no heat is lost to the surrounding) Specific heat capacity of water = 4.2 Jg-1k-1; Specific latent heat of fusion of ice = 336 Jg-1
key_points: Heat gained by ice (melting + warming) = heat lost by water
Solve to get x = 11°C
marking_schemes.model_answer: Heat gained by ice (to melt and then warm to final temp x) = Heat lost by water: 60×336 + 60×4.2×x = 140×4.2×(50−x). Simplifying: 60×4.2(80+x) = 140×4.2(50−x); 3(80+x) = 7(80−x); 240+3x = 350−7x; 10x = 110; x = 11°C. The final temperature is 11°C.
common_errors: Did not account for heat absorbed by melted ice to reach equilibrium temperature
Did not substitute change in temperature correctly
Did not write unit for final answer
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Give sufficient practice on numerical problems based on Calorimetry, including accounting for both latent heat and sensible heat.

marking_schemes.question_text: Draw a neat labeled diagram of a d.c. motor.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Diagram showing coil (armature with soft iron core) between field magnet poles N and S, connected via split rings S1, S2 with brushes B1, B2 to a D.C. supply with a variable resistor.
key_points: Field magnet with N and S poles shown
Armature coil with soft iron core between the poles
Split rings (commutator) with brushes, connected to D.C. supply
marking_schemes.model_answer: A labelled diagram of a d.c. motor shows an armature coil wound on a soft iron core placed between the N and S poles of a field magnet, connected via a split-ring commutator and brushes to a D.C. supply with a rheostat.
common_errors: Drew diagram of an A.C. generator instead
Did not label the diagram or labelled incorrectly
Drew slip rings instead of split rings
Drew the diagram with a load
Did not draw the field magnet
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Give sufficient practice to students in drawing diagrams; compare DC motor with AC generator while explaining.

marking_schemes.question_text: Write any one use of a d.c. motor.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Washing machine, mixers etc.
key_points: Used in devices like washing machine, mixer, toy fans, etc.
marking_schemes.model_answer: A d.c. motor is used in devices such as washing machines or mixers.
common_errors: Wrote 'energy conversion' as the answer instead of a use/application
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Differentiate between the function of a device (converting electrical to mechanical energy) and its usage (e.g., washing machine, mixer, toy fan).

marking_schemes.question_text: Differentiate between nuclear fusion and nuclear fission.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Combining two or more lighter nuclei to form a heavy nucleus is nuclear fusion whereas splitting a heavy nucleus into two or more lighter nuclei is nuclear fission.
key_points: Nuclear fusion: combining two or more lighter nuclei to form a heavier nucleus
Nuclear fission: splitting a heavy nucleus into two or more lighter nuclei
marking_schemes.model_answer: Nuclear fusion is the combining of two or more lighter nuclei to form a heavier nucleus, whereas nuclear fission is the splitting of a heavy nucleus into two or more lighter nuclei.
common_errors: Mixed up the definitions of fission and fusion
Used 'bigger' and 'smaller' instead of 'heavier' and 'lighter'
Gave vague statements such as 'large energy is given out during nuclear fusion' without comparing the quantity of nuclear material
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Explain the composition of elements explicitly with atomic and mass number when discussing fission and fusion.

marking_schemes.question_text: State one safety precaution in the disposal of nuclear waste.
marking_schemes.correct_answer: Should be disposed in thick lead casks away from colonies and deep into the earth.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Should be disposed in thick lead casks away from colonies and deep into the earth.
key_points: Nuclear waste should be disposed of in thick lead casks, away from colonies and buried deep in the earth
marking_schemes.model_answer: Nuclear waste should be disposed of in thick lead casks, buried deep in the earth and away from populated colonies.
common_errors: Gave precautions for handling radioactive substances instead of precautions specifically for waste disposal
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Instruct students that when a nucleus emits gamma radiation there is no change in mass/atomic number — relevant distinction from disposal precautions for waste handling.

marking_schemes.question_text: An atomic nucleus A is composed of 84 protons and 128 neutrons. The nucleus A emits an alpha particle and is transformed into a nucleus B. What is the composition of B?
marking_schemes.correct_answer: No. of protons = 82, No. of neutrons = 126
marking_schemes.scheme_text: The composition of B is No. of proton = 82, No of neutron = 126
key_points: Alpha emission reduces protons by 2 and neutrons by 2
B has 82 protons and 126 neutrons
marking_schemes.model_answer: Alpha emission removes 2 protons and 2 neutrons. So nucleus B has 82 protons and 126 neutrons.
common_errors: Did not write the number of neutrons
Forgot to add protons and neutrons to get mass number in a later part; subtracted 4 from neutron number and 2 from proton number instead of subtracting 4 from mass number
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Explain the change in atomic number and mass number during alpha decay with reactions.

marking_schemes.question_text: The nucleus B emits a beta particle and is transformed into a nucleus C. What is the composition of C?
marking_schemes.correct_answer: No. of protons = 83, No. of neutrons = 125
marking_schemes.scheme_text: The composition of C is No. of proton = 83, No. of neutron = 125
key_points: Beta emission increases protons by 1 and decreases neutrons by 1
C has 83 protons and 125 neutrons
marking_schemes.model_answer: Beta emission converts a neutron into a proton, increasing protons by 1 and decreasing neutrons by 1. So nucleus C has 83 protons and 125 neutrons.
common_errors: Used neutron number as atomic mass for beta emission incorrectly
Errors in first part propagated to this part since it depends on B's composition
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Explain the change in atomic number and mass number during beta decay with reactions.

marking_schemes.question_text: What is mass number of the nucleus A?
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Mass number of the nucleus A = 212.
key_points: Mass number = protons + neutrons = 84 + 128 = 212
marking_schemes.model_answer: Mass number of A = 84 protons + 128 neutrons = 212.
common_errors: Forgot to add the number of protons and neutrons
Wrote only the number of protons as the mass number
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Explain the composition of an element explicitly with atomic number and mass number.

marking_schemes.question_text: Does the composition of C change if it emits gamma radiations?
marking_schemes.correct_answer: No, the composition of a nucleus does not change if it emits gamma radiation.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: No, the composition of a nucleus does not change if it emits gamma radiation.
key_points: Gamma emission does not change the composition (protons/neutrons) of the nucleus
marking_schemes.model_answer: No, the composition of the nucleus does not change if it emits gamma radiation, since gamma rays are electromagnetic radiation with no mass or charge.
common_errors: A few candidates incorrectly answered 'Yes'
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Instruct students that when a nucleus emits gamma radiation, there is no change in the mass number and atomic number.
